title: 03 — A Framework for Design Reviews
html:
03 — A Framework for Design Reviews

The one idea: a good design discussion — a design review, an architecture decision, a whiteboard session with your team — is engineers working through an ambiguous problem together. What makes it productive is the order: pin down requirements before drawing boxes, agree on a high-level shape, then spend the time where the risk is.

1. The four steps and a time budget (for a 45–60 minute session)

---
title: Design review framework — four steps
---
flowchart LR
    A["1. Understand & scope<br/>5–10 min"] --> B["2. High-level design<br/>and agreement<br/>10–15 min"]
    B --> C["3. Deep dive<br/>15–25 min"]
    C --> D["4. Wrap up<br/>5 min"]

The same shape works for a one-page design doc: one section per step.

2. Step 1 — Understand the problem and establish scope

Don't draw anything yet. Ask:

Area Questions
Features What are the 2–3 features that matter most? What is explicitly out of scope?
Users How many (DAU)? Web, mobile, both? Internal or external?
Scale Expected growth in 1 year? 3 years? Read/write ratio?
Data Size of an item? Retention? Regulated or personal data?
Quality Latency targets? Consistency needs? Availability SLO?
Constraints Existing stack? Cloud provider? Build vs buy? Team skills? Deadline?

Then write the requirements down as two short lists — functional and non-functional — and do a quick estimate (→ chapter 02).

⚠️ The most common failure: solving immediately. A design that answers the wrong question is expensive precisely because it looks finished.

3. Step 2 — Propose a high-level design and get agreement

  1. API first — the 3–5 endpoints or operations that define the system.
  2. Boxes and arrows — clients, load balancer, services, data stores, cache, queue, CDN.
  3. Walk one or two use cases through the diagram end to end.
  4. Data model — main entities, keys, which store and why.
  5. Check in: "Does this look like a reasonable starting point before we go deeper?"

Keep it at the level of components. If it fits on one whiteboard, it's the right level.

4. Step 3 — Deep dive

Pick the 2–3 components that carry the most risk and go deep. Good deep-dive topics are usually one of:

  • The hot path (the operation with the highest QPS or tightest latency).
  • The hardest consistency problem (double booking, double spend, ordering).
  • The scaling bottleneck found in the estimate (a hot shard, fan-out).
  • A specific algorithm the problem hinges on (rate-limit algorithm, ID generation, geohash).

Let the group steer — the questions people ask are usually where the real risk is.

5. Step 4 — Wrap up

Useful things to cover at the end:

  • Bottlenecks and how you'd find them (what you'd monitor).
  • Failure modes — what happens when the cache, the queue or a region goes down.
  • Operational concerns — deploys, rollbacks, metrics, alerts.
  • Next scale step — what changes at 10× the load.
  • Decisions and open questions — written down, with owners. An architecture decision record (ADR) is a good home for them.

6. Do's and don'ts

Do Don't
Clarify and write down assumptions Jump to a solution
Think out loud Go silent for minutes
Offer options and pick one with a reason Present one option as the only option
Design for the stated scale Over-engineer for Google scale when the need is 10k users
Treat the discussion as collaboration Argue or get defensive
Name trade-offs explicitly Claim a design has no downsides
Go deep on the risky parts Spend 15 minutes on the login page

7. Phrases that keep a review productive

  • "Before I pick a store, let me list the access patterns."
  • "This is the one-way door in this design — I'd want to get the shard key right."
  • "We can accept eventual consistency here because…; we can't here because…"
  • "What I'd monitor first is… and the alert would fire on…"
  • "If the read/write ratio flipped, I'd change X to Y."

8. .NET / Azure mapping

Naming concrete components the team can operate is more useful than generic boxes:

Generic box Concrete choice to name
API service ASP.NET Core minimal APIs / controllers on App Service or AKS
API gateway Azure API Management (rate limits, auth, versioning)
Relational DB Azure SQL (with EF Core or Dapper)
NoSQL Cosmos DB
Cache Azure Cache for Redis
Queue / events Service Bus / Event Hubs
Background workers BackgroundService / Azure Functions
Object storage + CDN Blob Storage + Front Door
Search Azure AI Search

9. Review checklist

  • Functional + non-functional requirements written.
  • Estimate done and its implication stated.
  • API defined before the diagram.
  • One use case walked end to end.
  • 2–3 deep dives on the riskiest parts.
  • Failure modes, monitoring and next-scale step covered.
  • Decisions and open questions recorded.
